sections.title: In one minute
items: GitHub Actions is a CI/CD platform that runs workflows when something happens in a repository, such as a push or a pull request. It also runs on a schedule, from the API, or by hand.

cards.title: Workflow
cards.text: A YAML file in `.github/workflows` that runs one or more jobs

cards.title: Event
cards.text: An activity that triggers a run: a push, a pull request, an issue, a schedule, a manual dispatch

cards.title: Job
cards.text: A set of steps that run on the same runner. Jobs run in parallel unless one `needs` another

cards.title: Step
cards.text: A shell command or an action, run in order inside a job

cards.title: Action
cards.text: A reusable unit of code that a step runs with `uses`

cards.title: Runner
cards.text: The machine that runs a job. Each runner runs one job at a time

items.alt: An event triggers a workflow. The workflow has jobs. Each job runs on a runner and has steps. A step runs a command or an action.
items.caption: How the parts fit. Jobs run in parallel unless a job needs another.

sections.title: The smallest workflow
items: Workflow files must have a `.yml` or `.yaml` extension and live in the `.github/workflows` directory of the repository.
A job runs inside its own virtual machine, or inside a container. Each workflow run uses a fresh, newly provisioned machine on GitHub-hosted runners.

sections.title: The events you use most

rows: A commit or tag is pushed
Runs by default for `opened`, `synchronize` and `reopened`. `GITHUB_SHA` is the last merge commit, `GITHUB_REF` is `refs/pull/<n>/merge`
Same default types, but runs the workflow and code from the default branch (last commit on the default branch). See the gotcha below
A manual run, from the UI, API or `gh`
Optional `inputs`. Only receives events when the file is on the default branch
Another workflow requested, started or completed
Types: `completed`, `requested`, `in_progress`. Only runs if the file is on the default branch. No more than three levels of chaining
POSIX cron, UTC by default, at most every 5 minutes. Runs on the default branch's latest commit
A call to the REST API
Custom `event_type`, filtered with `types`. Default branch only
Types include `published`, `created`, `released`, `prereleased`. Not for `created`, `edited` or `deleted` on a draft release

There is no `pull_request_comment` event: use `issue_comment`.

sections.title: Order and conditions
items: Jobs have no dependencies by default and run in parallel. `needs` makes a job wait. If a job fails or is skipped, every job that needs it is skipped too, unless it has an `if` such as `always()` that lets it continue.
`jobs.<job_id>.if` is evaluated before the matrix is applied, so it cannot read `matrix` values.

sections.title: runs-on
items: `runs-on` can be a string, a variable, an array, or a mapping with `group` or `labels`. An array means the runner must have all of the labels.

items.title: A self-hosted runner with three labels

items: The labels of the GitHub-hosted runners are on the [Runners](#runners) page.

sections.title: Outputs, containers and services
items: `jobs.<job_id>.outputs` is a map. Downstream jobs read it through the `needs` context. Outputs are limited to 1 MB per job and 50 MB per run; an output that contains a secret is redacted and not sent.

`container` runs the job's steps in a container (`image`, `credentials`, `env`, `ports`, `volumes`, `options`). `services` starts service containers beside the job, each with `image`, `credentials`, `env`, `ports`, `volumes`, `options`, `command` and `entrypoint`.

sections.title: Failure and time

rows: Cancel the job after this many minutes. Default 360. The runner's own limit applies if it is lower
Let the workflow run pass when this job fails. In a matrix it affects that one job
In a matrix, cancel the other jobs when one fails. Default true

items: The `GITHUB_TOKEN` expires when the job finishes or after at most 24 hours.

sections.title: uses
items: `uses` runs an action from the same repository, a public repository, or a Docker image. Name the version: a Git ref, a commit SHA or a Docker tag. Without one, an update by the action's owner can break your workflow.

items.text: The commit SHA of a released version is the safest choice for stability and security.

sections.title: Background steps
items: `background: true` starts a step asynchronously, so the job moves on without waiting. Use it for databases, servers or monitors that must run beside later steps. Give it an `id` so a later step can wait for it or cancel it.
At most 10 background steps run at once in one job; the rest queue until a slot is free. Works for `run` and `uses` steps.

sections.title: How it works
items: `concurrency` keeps at most one running job or workflow per group. A group can be any string or expression. At workflow level the expression can use only the `github`, `inputs` and `vars` contexts. The key also exists on a job.

By default a new run waits as pending, and replaces any older pending run in the same group (which is cancelled). Add `cancel-in-progress: true` to also cancel the run that is already running. `cancel-in-progress` can be an expression.

items.title: Cancel older runs of the same ref

sections.title: Rules
items: An optional `queue` setting lets more than one run wait in the same group: the page describes it (unconfirmed here).

items.text: With a reusable workflow, do not use the same group name in the caller and the called workflow together with `cancel-in-progress: true`: the running workflow would be cancelled.

sections.title: Basics
items: Write an expression as `${{ <expression> }}`. In an `if` you may leave the braces out. Quote a string with single quotes; a literal single quote is written twice. Double quotes are an error.
In a condition, `false`, `0`, `-0`, `''` and `null` are false; everything else is true.

sections.title: Operators
items: Comparisons are loose. If the types differ, both sides are turned into numbers: null becomes 0, true 1, false 0, a string is parsed as a JSON number or becomes NaN (an empty string is 0), arrays and objects become NaN. A comparison with NaN is false. Strings are compared without regard to case. Objects and arrays are equal only if they are the same instance.

sections.title: Functions

rows: True if the string contains the substring, or the array has the item. Not case sensitive
Replace `{0}`, `{1}` in the string. Escape braces by doubling them
Join array values into a string. The default separator is `,`
A pretty-printed JSON string. Useful to debug a context
Turn a JSON string into an object, array, number or boolean
One SHA-256 for the files that match. Paths are inside `GITHUB_WORKSPACE`; `!` excludes
A conditional function. Its syntax is on the expressions page (unconfirmed here)

items: An object filter such as `github.event.issue.labels.*.name` reads one property from every item of an array.
Values are cast to strings for some functions: null becomes `''`, a boolean `'true'` or `'false'`; arrays and objects are not converted.

sections.title: Status checks for if

rows: All previous steps succeeded. It is the default when an `if` has no status function
Any previous step of the job failed. In dependent jobs, any ancestor job failed

items: Outside an `if`, read the job status with `job.status`.

items.text: Do not use `always()` for a step that can fail critically, such as getting the sources: the workflow may hang until it times out. Use `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` to run a step whatever the result.
`steps.<id>.outputs.<name>` is always a string. Compare numbers with `fromJSON(...)`.

sections.title: Reusable workflows
items: A reusable workflow is a workflow with `on: workflow_call`. It declares `inputs` (each with a `type`), `outputs` and `secrets`. A caller runs it as a job with `uses`.

rows: A workflow in the same repository
A workflow in another repository. The ref is a SHA, a release tag or a branch

items: `secrets: inherit` passes every secret the caller can access, including across repositories of one organization or enterprise.

sections.title: What the calling job can set
items: Only these keys are allowed on a job that calls a reusable workflow: `name`, `uses`, `with`, `secrets`, `strategy`, `needs`, `if`, `concurrency`, `permissions` and `cache-mode`.

rows: Up to ten levels of workflows
At most 50 unique reusable workflows from one workflow file, including nested ones
Not shared either way. Pass values as inputs, or read outputs, or use `vars`
Cannot pass values to the caller's steps: the call is a job, not a step
The called workflow can only downgrade the `GITHUB_TOKEN`
GitHub-hosted runners are chosen from the caller's context and billed to the caller
None: if an action or workflow is renamed or moved, workflows that use the old name fail

rows: `composite`, a Node.js version such as `node24`, or `docker`
The steps of a composite action

items: The metadata file can have another name than `action.yml`: the page says how.

sections.title: Composite actions
items: A composite action groups steps (`runs.using: composite`, `runs.steps`) so a workflow can use them in one step with `uses`. It is defined in an `action.yml` file, not in `.github/workflows`.

notes: The docs pages show no version or date. They were read on 2026-11-03; a later change on GitHub's side is not detected by `make check`.
The Node.js version in an action's `runs.using` changes over time. The example on the metadata page used `node24` when it was read.

compare.text: A composite action is used from a step (`steps[*].uses`); a reusable workflow is used from a job (`jobs.<id>.uses`).

sections.title: GitHub-hosted runners
items: A GitHub-hosted runner is a virtual machine that GitHub provides. Each workflow run gets a new machine, except the single-CPU `ubuntu-slim`, which is a container. The `-latest` labels are the newest stable images GitHub provides, which may not be the newest version of the operating system.
The labels and sizes differ for private repositories: the runners reference has a table for each.

items.text: Beta and deprecated images are provided as is and are outside the service level agreement.

sections.title: Self-hosted runners
items: A self-hosted runner is a machine you run. It gets the labels `self-hosted`, its operating system and its architecture automatically; you can add more. `runs-on` with several labels selects a runner that has all of them.
To run Docker container actions or service containers, the machine must be Linux with Docker installed. The runner application itself needs few resources.

Supported systems include several Linux distributions (Ubuntu 20.04 and later, Debian 10 and later, RHEL 8 and later, and others) and Windows 10 and 11 and Windows Server: the reference has the full list and the processor architectures.

sections.title: Autoscaling
items: Actions Runner Controller runs runners on Kubernetes. The GitHub Actions Runner Scale Set Client is a client for building your own autoscaler. Ephemeral runners take one job and are then removed, which suits autoscaling. Runner software updates and webhooks for autoscaling are described on the self-hosted reference.

sections.title: Choosing
items: The Compare tab has GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners side by side.

entries.summary: The GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets, OIDC, script injection and third-party actions: the rules that matter most.

started.basis: Not stated on the pages read

cncf.text: A commercial service from GitHub, not a CNCF project.

version.name: GitHub Actions (GitHub Docs)
version.docs: docs.github.com/en/actions, the pages named in sources, read 2026-11-03; the pages show no version or date

sections.title: Secrets

rows: Letters, digits and underscores. Not starting with `GITHUB_` or a number. Case-insensitive, stored in uppercase
Environment beats repository beats organization when names match
1,000 organization secrets, 100 repository secrets, 100 environment secrets. 48 KB each
Organization and repository secrets when the run is queued; environment secrets when a job that uses the environment starts

items: Use one secret per value. Structured values such as a JSON blob defeat redaction, because redaction needs an exact match.
Redaction is done by the runner. If a secret reached a log unredacted, delete the log and rotate the secret.

sections.title: Script injection
items: An expression such as `${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}` is replaced before the script runs, so a crafted value becomes part of the script. Pass untrusted input through an environment variable, or to an action as an input.

sections.title: OpenID Connect
items: Instead of a stored cloud credential, a job can request a short-lived OIDC token and exchange it with the cloud provider. The job or workflow needs `id-token: write`. That permission only allows fetching the token; it grants no write access to anything else.

The token is requested with the `getIDToken()` method of the Actions toolkit, or with the `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL` and `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN` variables. The cloud role trusts claims such as the subject, which can name an environment, a branch, a tag or a pull request.
Give the `GITHUB_TOKEN` the least access: default to read-only and raise it per job ([Permissions](#permissions))
Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA, and keep them up to date (Dependabot version updates can do this)
Never put secrets in plain text in workflow files; mask other sensitive values with `::add-mask::`
Register any value derived from a secret as a secret too, including Base64 and URL-encoded forms
Require reviewers on environments that hold production secrets ([Environments](#environments))
Use CODEOWNERS on the workflow files, and code scanning and OpenSSF Scorecards for the workflows themselves
Do not check out untrusted pull request code in a privileged trigger such as `pull_request_target`
Review run logs after testing valid and invalid inputs: tools can print secrets in error messages

notes: The docs pages show no version or date. They were read on 2026-11-03; a later change on GitHub's side is not detected by `make check`.

sections.title: What an environment does
items: A job names an environment with `jobs.<job_id>.environment`: a name, or a name and a `url`. The job then follows the environment's rules and can use its secrets and variables. A deployment is recorded.

rows: Up to six users or teams. One approval is enough. You can prevent the person who started the deployment from approving it
Delay the job by 1 to 43,200 minutes (30 days). The wait is not billed
No restriction, protected branches only, or selected name patterns, matched against `GITHUB_REF`
Environment secrets are read when a job that uses the environment starts. They beat repository secrets of the same name

items: A run can wait for environment approval for up to 30 days.

items.text: On GitHub Free, Pro and Team plans, required reviewers and wait timers are available only for public repositories.
A tag with the same name as a protected branch, and forks with a matching branch name, cannot deploy to the environment.

version.name: GitHub Actions (GitHub Docs)
version.docs: docs.github.com/en/actions, the pages named in sources, read 2026-11-03; the pages show no version or date

rows: Files a job produces that you want after the run, or to pass to another job: binaries, logs, test results
Files that rarely change between runs: downloaded dependencies, intermediate build output
A cache action with a `key` and optional `restore-keys`
A job should still work on a cache miss

sections.title: Cache keys
items: The cache action looks for an exact match of the `key` in the branch of the run, then partial matches of the key, then each `restore-keys` entry in order. A key can use contexts and functions, for example a hash of a lock file.

items.title: Restore keys, from the most to the least specific

sections.title: Limits

rows: A cache entry not accessed for over 7 days is removed
10 GB by default, raisable by owners and administrators. Use beyond it is billed
The new cache is saved and older ones are evicted until the total is under the limit. Constant eviction is cache thrashing
200 uploads and 1,500 downloads per minute per repository

items: `cache-mode` (`read`, `write`, `write-only`, `none`) limits cache access per workflow or job. If you omit it, a default based on the trigger applies.

items.text: Setting `cache-mode: write` or `write-only` on a low-trust trigger can bypass the read-only default and reintroduce cache poisoning.

sections.title: Provenance
items: Artifact attestations create provenance and integrity guarantees for what you build, so consumers can verify where and how it was built. They need the `attestations` and `id-token` permissions.

notes: The docs pages show no version or date. They were read on 2026-11-03; a later change on GitHub's side is not detected by `make check`.
Artifact retention and size limits are on the artifacts pages and are not repeated here.
That attestations need both `attestations` and `id-token` write permission is inferred from the permissions list and the OIDC page: confirm on the attestations how-to (unconfirmed here).
